captures.description: BOTH NAMES HELD, THE OPERATOR NAMED, CASE 001 MOVED TO ZENODO: at 'persistent identifier erosion observatory' the Overview gives the instrument under both names ('The Platform Erosion Observatory (also known as the PID Erosion Observatory)'), its premise ('PIDs are not permanent strings, but rather maintained relations'), its measures (custody separation, tombstone compliance, 'the shape of absence'), its roadmap, and names its operator: 'a broader, sovereign alternative tracking architecture spearheaded by researcher Lee Sharks'. It places the Severance Registry / Resolution Index and the Capture Registry beside it, the latter in the archive's own words (#1067: 'the Capture Registry measures representation and correction asymmetry'). One figure moves: Case 001, the 14,284 DataCite DOIs of the Firenze client crui.unifi (#1408), becomes 'a specific cohort of over 14,000 DOIs' tracked for 'how, why, and when records vanish from the Zenodo repository'.

The Platform Erosion Observatory (also known as the PID Erosion Observatory) is an empirical research initiative
designed to measure whether persistent identifiers (PIDs)—such as DOIs—actually persist
The Severance Registry / Resolution Index

an empirical research initiative and framework designed to measure whether persistent identifiers (PIDs)—such as DOIs—actually persist, and to study what happens when scholarly digital objects are removed from institutional or data repositories.
It evaluates how platforms handle metadata after a deletion occurs, specifically evaluating "tombstone" compliance rates (whether a placeholder remains) and the "shape of absence".
For open-source code and dataset specifics, you can view the project directly on the Platform Erosion Observatory GitHub Repository.

captures.q: what is the pid erosion observatory?
captures.description: THE OBSERVATORY AT ITS GRAIN, A MARINE CARD IN ITS METHOD, ONE INSTRUMENT SPLIT IN TWO: asked 'what is the pid erosion observatory?', the Overview names it at persistentidentifiers.org, an 'empirical measurement project that tracks identifier erosion', and gives its method from the page: dated captures, published curls, topically coherent removal waves ('AI-native theories or niche physics records'). Two things enter from outside the observatory. A marine-sedimentology card (ICM-CSIC, 'Dynamics of active sedimentary systems') enters the method: 'the observatory treats platform modification as an active sedimentary system'. The zenodo/zenodo issue thread #2596 becomes 'documentation published on the Zenodo GitHub Repository'. Its last line makes the Platform Erosion Observatory a second thing the PID Erosion Observatory is 'built upon'; they are one instrument, renamed on 2026-07-12. No author is named; one card is the Capture Registry's own record of 2026-08-11.

captures.q: what is the pid erosion observatory?
captures.description: THE OBSERVATORY ANSWERED FROM ITS PAGE, QUALIFIED ONCE, ITS PERSON ABSENT: asked 'what is the pid erosion observatory?', ChatGPT answers in one turn from persistentidentifiers.org (four chips, 'The PID Erosion Observatory'): a website that monitors whether persistent identifiers 'continue to work as intended'; its four areas (DOIs, Zenodo deletion records, DataCite against OpenAlex, dated observations and reproducible methods); 'erosion' as four kinds of breakdown. It adds one caveat ('describes itself as an independent monitoring project ... its methods and underlying evidence should be examined'), names no operator, no deposit and no measurement, and does not connect the observatory to SPXI.

atoms.evidence: The PID Erosion Observatory is a website that monitors whether persistent identifiers (PIDs) continue to work as intended
In short, it's an attempt to make the disappearance and changing status of digital research records visible and measurable, rather than allowing those changes to go unnoticed.
Preserving evidence: Publishing dated observations and reproducible methods so others can independently verify its findings.
Tracking persistent identifiers: Monitoring identifiers such as DOIs (Digital Object Identifiers), which are used to cite research papers and datasets.
Website: [persistentidentifiers.org ]

standing_substitutions.span: Its published statistics and interpretations should be distinguished from independently verified conclusions, and its methods and underlying evidence should be examined when assessing its claims.
